q: How do royalties move with a $10/bbl Brent change?

r.response:
Royalties are price-linked: a $10/bbl Brent increase adds about $21.0B of revenue and $4.2B of royalties and production taxes (20% of the incremental upstream revenue).

• Net of royalties, operating income rises about $16.8B before hedges
• Trading-book hedge settlements give back about $2.4B
• After 46% effective tax, net income rises about $7.8B

The tiered royalty rate steps up above $70 and $100 Brent, so the take increases slightly at higher prices.

q: If Brent drops to $55/bbl, what happens to FY2026 EBITDA and free cash flow?

r.response:
If Brent drops to $55/bbl from the $75 budget deck — other levers unchanged — FY2026 EBITDA falls from $213.8B to $185.0B (−$28.8B) and net income from $101.7B to $86.1B.

• Revenue −$37.2B: −$42.0B on price, partly offset by +$4.8B of hedge settlements on the trading book
• Royalties fall with price (−$8.4B), cushioning the hit
• Free cash flow drops from $60.3B to about $44.8B after $51.2B capex

No asset turns cash-negative: onshore crude still earns over $50/bbl of netback at $55 Brent. The gap to the $83.7B dividend widens to about $39B. I can push this to a new scenario version.

q: Does free cash flow cover the dividend at $60 Brent?

r.response:
Not fully — even in the budget. The FY2026 dividend (base plus performance-linked) is $83.7B against free cash flow of $60.3B, so about $23B is funded from cash and debt.

• At $60 Brent, net income falls by $11.7B and free cash flow to about $48.6B — the gap widens to about $35B
• Cash falls from $95.7B to $62.0B through FY2026 in the budget; at $60 Brent it would end near $50B
• Gearing stays low: bonds and sukuk of $166B against equity of $214B

Options: phase $5–8B of gas expansion capex into FY2027, or size the performance-linked dividend to free cash flow.
